posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
There are a couple of ways to do this. The easiest is to light the microscope with one or more lightings. Place a transparency under the microscope and lit it from underneath (ie have a lighting from beneath so that the light goes through the shaft of the microscope) The magnified transparency can now be seen by a real viewer through the eyepiece of the real microscope. Since this is real light, it'll show up on the hologram. Thus the illuminated microscope will become a hologram of a microscope, because that's how you lit it, and the image of the magnified transparency as seen through the microscope wll be seen "through" the eyepiece of the holographic image of the microscope. If you place your eye at the eyepiece of the image, you'll see what you would have seen through the real thing simply because what the plate sees is what you see. Think of it as a memory of all you saw had your face been in the plate holder at the time you shot the hologram.

posts.author: DJ Mathson
posts.content_md: I think the microscope hologram is made with the "key hole" technique. One way to do this: You make one master hologram of the microscope, and one master of the object that is to be seen through the eyepiece. Then make a second master where you first make an exposure from the microscope master with the eyepiece aligned to the second master plate and with the area of the eyepiece masked off. Then make a second exposure from the master of the object with everything exept the eyepiece area masked off. Then you can transfer this second master to a new hologram.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:c2e9381a00="DJ Mathson"]I think the microscope hologram is made with the "key hole" technique. One way to do this: You make one master hologram of the microscope, and one master of the object that is to be seen through the eyepiece. Then make a second master where you first make an exposure from the microscope master with the eyepiece aligned to the second master plate and with the area of the eyepiece masked off. Then make a second exposure from the master of the object with everything exept the eyepiece area masked off. Then you can transfer this second master to a new hologram.[/quote:c2e9381a00]

As I understand it, you're basically seeing the object to be seen through the microscope through an aperture of the eyepiece created by the masks. In this case there won't be any magnification of the object, since the light from the object will not have gone through the lenses of the microscope. I have a similar piece of a telescope trained on a distant house. When seen from a distance, you can't make out any detail of the house. When you place your eye to the eyepiece of the telescope, you can see a couple in the window of the house.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I assume the idea is that you'd use a single lens and a dedicated H1 to simulate the magnification of the miscroscope. This would probably be a better way of doing it because the image in a real microscope is virtual. Also, you're expected to put your eye right into the eyepiece which then blocks off stray light, whereas a holographic eyepiece will not block stray light. In my original reply, I gave the "easiest" method of doing this, which was intended to be a sort of: "here's one way of doing it". I thought that no-one had replied to Nick about the hows and whys of these type of images and gave a broad overview. If I were actually trying to do it, I'd have a real image (from maybe a curved mirror) project where the virtual image would have been in a real microscope and create a seperate H1 just for that. The aperture would have nbeen much larger than a real microscope aperture, but the ligth gathering power would also be greater and the leeway in eye position would be better.

Actually Nick I will let you into a secret about Kaveh, because it should'nt be secret ,

he deserves credit for it.

In the great Science Museum at South Kensington , London, up on the top floor there is an Optics section. There are some fine holograms up there on display and one of the most interesting is made by Kaveh. It was of a stuffed animal -a baby alligator I think or it may have been a croc. but whatever it was it was obviously sufficiently non-cuddly and non-cute to have once passed Kaveh's stern non-Kitch test. (At least I find it beautiful)

The hologram is a transmission HIG (Holographic Image Generator) which has depth, this means you have to have the light the other side of the plate to yourself and the light needs to be monochromatic to see it clearly. This hologram demonstrates beautifully why the light needs to be monochromatic and also an additional weird effect if you don't display a transmission HIG in the same color as you made it in.

It is displayed in the glass case with a small point-source mercury lamp shining through the plate towards you. The thing about this lamp is that it has 3 distinct

colors which are fairly monochromatic. Violet, green and red.

This produces the weird effect of creating 3 distinct partially overlapping alligators in each colour.

The red one being closest to the plate and the violet one being not only furthest from the plate but also sightly longer and thinner, the green one being intermediate in all respects. So how can one set of fringes produced by one object finish up replaying 3 objects depending on your reconstructing light color. You can understand now why

you cannot use a white light to replay the HIG or you just get a rainbow fuzz of multiple alligators. I hope someone out there can point you to a good website that explains some of this with animations. There are always those old fashioned books of course, the best I think being by Graham Saxby. 

jeff

 I've often noted that the very basics of interference, diffraction and aberations are difficult to understand by many because they're explained in the semi-scientific jargon that usually most people find confusing to begin with. Even (especially!) college lecturers suffer from this inability to explain in simple terms. It took me quite a while to translate y=sin(x) where x is an angle to "a wave is decribed by psi = sin(kx-wt) where kx-wt is the phase". I first heard this in A level Physics (roughly 17 years old) and finally it hit me in first-year undergrad (approx 19 years old) that "phase" simply meant the value of the sin and all you needed to do was convert one number (kx-wt) to an angle by descriibing length in segments of wavelength and time in segments of the period and simply multiplying by 360. Simple! Yet it took me two years to understand this because this word 'phase' was thrown off as if I was born with an understanding of it. I'm planning to put up a series animations in various 3D programs I have, converted to video, to show these more fully and intuitively.

Jeff, I had forgotten about that hologram in the science museum. I wonder if it is still there. Yes, I wanted to show why you can't show a normal transmission hologram in broadband light and I think we used a mercury lamp to show the image in different colors and different positions. It showed dispersion quite well.

Talking about museums and talking about cheap looking holograms, I was in Boston a few weeks ago and went into the museum of science. I looked for holograms and I saw a few barely visible film holograms in a throw-away corner which was not going to inspire anyone to try and make a holgoram. Now that's what I would call cheap and nasty.
